newsitem.title: MALAYSIA: Malaysia seen signalling freer press.
newsitem.headline: Malaysia seen signalling freer press.

text.p: Malaysia's announcement that it will withdraw the national news agency's rights to distribute foreign news signals a freer press in a country with a poor image on the issue, analysts said on Thursday.

Information Minister Mohamed Rahmat said after a cabinet meeting on Wednesday that the government would introduce legislation in parliament ending the Bernama news agency's right to distribute foreign news in the country.

That monopoly has allowed Bernama to collect fees from news agencies such as Reuters, the Associated Press, Agence France-Presse and Bloomberg, among others. It has collected a percentage of the foreign agencies' revenues for distributing their news to the Malaysian print and broadcast media.
The exclusive rights were given to Bernama in 1984 by an act of parliament, primarily to provide it with additional revenue and not for censorship purposes, Mohamed told reporters.
"We feel it's no longer necessary as we want to ensure a free flow of information. If Bernama suffers a loss due to this move, we will make up for it through other means," he said.
Bernama is scheduled to be corporatised by the end of the year, the first step toward its ultimate privatisation.

"This thing has been like an albatross around our neck," Bernama Chief Editor Syed Jamil Jaafar told Reuters. "We've been trying to wean ourselves (off news agency revenues) for years. We knew it was coming sooner or later. It just came sooner than we expected."
The agency fees accounted for 20 percent of Bernama's revenues, about eight million ringgit ($3.2 million), he said.

Several Asian governments give their national news agencies the right to control distribution of foreign news -- and collect fees -- in order to screen out, at least in theory, stories deemed too sensitive for local consumption.
They include Xinhua of China, South Korea's Yonhap news agency, Indonesia's Antara, the Press Trust of India and the Vietnam News Agency.
Indonesia's newly-installed Information Minister Gen. Hartono said he was not familiar with the issue.

"I don't know about that (Malaysia's move)," Hartono said. "I think if it is good for the nation, and ASEAN (the Association of South East Asian Nations), then it can be considered. I don't know about it as I have just newly been promoted. My speciality is the army."

In China, the official Xinhua news agency controls distribution of news from foreign agencies to domestic media clients. Early last year it was granted sweeping powers to regulate the supply of financial news to Chinese customers.
Officials of the Communist Party-controlled agency on Thursday declined to comment on their plans to regulate the supply of news by overseas companies.

Xinhua said last month it had withdrawn a plan to impose a fee on foreign financial news organisations, but that it would supervise their activities as mandated under a 1996 central government edict issued in the name of state security.

The edict, which threatens punishment for news vendors whose information "slanders China", banned domestic organisations from buying economic information directly from foreign sources and gave Xinhua the power to determine subscription rates.

A survey of expatriate businessmen published last week by the Political & Economic Risk Consultancy ranked Malaysia near the bottom of Asian countries in terms of perceived press freedom. Only Singapore and China were ranked lower.

Senior government officials in Malaysia have said privately that the Bernama arrangement sent "all the wrong signals" when the government is promoting its Multimedia Super Corridor (MSC) and assuring investors of an uncensored information superhighway.

A brainchild of Prime Minister Mahathir Mohamad, the MSC is a 15- by 50-km (nine- by 30-mile) zone stretching south from Kuala Lumpur to where a "cyberspace" international airport and a new federal "paperless" capital are being built.

"In a way it is a good development," Bernama's Syed Jamil said. "The Prime Minister has been going around promoting the MSC and saying it will have a free flow of information. Now we are doing what we are saying."
Analysts said the end to Bernama's role in foreign news recognises that the age of the Internet and satellite broadcasting makes traditional censorship impractical.
"I think it's a good sign," said political columnist Rustan Sani of the government's announcement.
"We're moving toward a greater sense of tolerance. I think (the repeal of) this law is a signal that things are changing. We need more signals," he said.
